detail.scope: Commercial-sector electricity sales and average price by state, as reported to EIA. Data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, so this is a proxy for their load, not a measurement of it.

sources.name: ERCOT
sources.scope: Large generators with a full interconnection study requested, from the monthly Generator Interconnection Status report for Texas. Includes projects from study through commissioning.

sources.name: NYISO
sources.scope: Projects in the New York interconnection queue as NYISO publishes them.

sources.name: MISO
sources.scope: Projects in the Midcontinent generator interconnection queue, all statuses as MISO publishes them.

sources.name: Southwest Power Pool
sources.scope: Generator interconnection requests across the south-central US, all statuses as SPP publishes them, withdrawn requests counted separately.

sources.name: CAISO
sources.scope: Active generator interconnection requests on the California ISO grid, from the public queue report. Completed and withdrawn projects are counted separately.

analysis.body:
# Grid Interconnection and AI Data Center Power

The continental US grid interconnection queues tracked by EIA and four major grid operators totaled 1.327 million MW of planned generation and storage as of mid-September 2026, with Texas alone accounting for 438,086 MW through ERCOT. Storage capacity in those queues reached 328,106 MW cumulatively across all operators, while solar and wind together represented 398,165 MW. These queues reflect projects in all stages from early study through near-completion, not imminent capacity, but the composition signals infrastructure alignment with sustained high power demand. Commercial-sector electricity sales across eight major states hit 54,797 MWh in June 2026, with Texas consuming 15,754 MWh at $8.66 per MWh, while California consumed 10,025 MWh at $27.33 per MWh—a price spread reflecting both generation scarcity and regional grid constraints.

The growth in queued storage and gas-fired generation tracks the patterns expected from data center load concentration in certain regions. ERCOT's queue included 78,092 MW of gas capacity and 159,820 MW of storage, proportionally higher than other operators, while California's queue showed the heaviest weighting toward storage (46,944 MW) and solar (18,896 MW) relative to its smaller total queue size of 71,682 MW. NYISO's queue contained 319,095 MW nominally, but 291,136 MW was classified as "other" fuel type—a category that obscures the actual generation mix. Across MISO, SPP, and ERCOT, solar and wind projects dominated by count and raw capacity, yet gas and storage grew as proportions of total MW, reflecting the intermittency challenge posed by distributed renewable demand.

California's electricity price of $27.33 per MWh in June remained the highest among the eight states, nearly triple Texas's rate, while commercial load in Virginia and Arizona was substantially smaller than in the major load centers despite similar per-MWh pricing to Texas. Watch the next quarterly EIA commercial sales report and any announced delays or withdrawals in the ERCOT and CAISO queues, as those will signal whether planned supply is tracking actual data center and hyperscale deployment pace.
